The bleeding also caused hypotension and injury to the heart, likely due to demand ischemia from the blood loss.

During hospitalization, the patient developed ventricular tachycardia, which can be a life-threatening heart rhythm. The patient was discharged home with a lifevest, which is worn externally and will shock the patient if this dangerous rhythm occurs again. Additionally, Metoprolol succinate was started to help lower heart rate and blood pressure by taking some of the workload off the heart.

Following aortic surgery, the patient experienced postoperative confusion and agitation, which was treated with Haldol and Zyprexa. Psychiatry and social work were consulted to evaluate postoperative confusion with hallucinations. The patient remained in the CVICU until his mental status improved. His mental status returned to baseline, and he was cleared for discharge on postoperative day 9.

The patient has an anoxic brain injury from a cardiac arrest during a procedure, with stable reduction in gray-white differentiation on CT head and mild to moderate encephalopathy on EEG without epileptiform discharges. He has a tracheostomy and PEG tube for feeding. He developed tongue lacerations from biting, requiring total teeth extraction, and MRSA bacteremia requiring 4 weeks of vancomycin. He was discharged to extended care facility for ongoing management.

The patient was initially treated with levofloxacin and Unasyn to cover for aspiration and community-acquired pneumonia. Coverage was broadened to vancomycin and Zosyn on hospital day 3. After completing a week of antibiotics, she remained persistently febrile, so antibiotics were held. The patient is currently being treated with multi-drug therapy for presumed pleural tuberculosis, and fever has improved since induction of TB therapy.

The patient's intracerebral hemorrhage was treated conservatively with blood pressure control and monitoring. He was offered a Factor VII trial but refused, and there were no other alternative therapies indicated. His blood pressure was initially controlled with a labetalol drip for a goal systolic blood pressure less than 140, and aspirin and heparin products were held given the hemorrhage. The acute renal failure likely started from poor forward flow from initial cardiogenic failure and was probably exacerbated by 320 ccs of contrast received in the catheterization lab. She developed muddy brown casts on urine analysis and due to hyperkalemia to 6.8 and anuria immediately post catheterization, she was treated with dialysis for volume overload and hyperkalemia. She is likely now dialysis-dependent with oliguria.

The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy for necrotic uterus with abscess, then required a second operation for perforated diverticulitis with pelvic peritonitis, requiring colon resection and colostomy placement. She developed polymicrobial sepsis with bacteremia but is slowly getting better with stable vital signs and decreasing white blood cell count on intravenous antibiotics. At discharge, she was afebrile, tolerating regular diet, ambulating with assistance, and recommended for rehabilitation for continued recovery.

The patient's pain was well controlled with Percocet (oxycodone-acetaminophen 5-325 mg) at discharge. She was prescribed 1-2 tablets every 4-6 hours as needed for pain, to be taken with food. Additionally, acetaminophen 325 mg (two tablets every 4-6 hours as needed) was available for pain management. The patient was instructed not to take Percocet with Ativan concurrently.

The bleeding gums in this patient were caused by thrombocytopenia, with platelet counts as low as 45K. The patient has several reasons for low platelets including end-stage liver disease, splenomegaly, critical illness, and myelosuppressive antibiotics. Aminocaproic acid was used for gum bleeding and prescribed at discharge for application to gums as needed. There is no mention of oral cancer or concerns for malignancy in the medical record.
